title: How Street Gangs Work
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss how street gangs work: FBI membership figures (2005 vs. 2011 National Gang Threat Assessment), whether gang problems are overstated, and economic causes such as unemployment and the economic crisis. They cover why people join (poverty, peer pressure, boredom, belonging, gang-run community programs), gang history from 19th-century New York ethnic gangs (Five Points) and 1950s-60s car clubs to the Crips and Bloods in Los Angeles, the Watts Truce, the People and Folk nations, the role of drugs and the crack era in Chicago's Black Gangster Disciples, prison gangs, female and co-ed gangs, hybrid gangs, sister gangs, Native American and immigrant gangs, gang initiations, leaving a gang, the FBI's list of dangerous gangs, and anti-gang programs like weed and seed. Ends with listener mail about a young mother who gave birth at age five.

segments.title: Opening banter and gang myths
segments.summary: Hosts joke about the show not being affiliated with any gang, then discuss how gangs have shifted away from spray-painting tags toward more sophisticated crimes like mortgage fraud and identity theft.

segments.title: Gang membership numbers and the economic crisis
segments.summary: Josh cites FBI National Gang Threat Assessment figures: about 731,000 gang members in 2005 and 1.4 million in 2011, with gangs rising from 27,000 to 33,000 (the 2005 figure is stated as roughly 27,000 gangs). They speculate that federal grants may inflate numbers and that the economic crisis drove membership up.

segments.title: Poverty, unemployment and gang homicides
segments.summary: The hosts discuss poverty and lack of economic opportunity as drivers of gang membership, citing a Los Angeles study linking neighborhoods with 14 to 16 percent unemployment to about fifteen times more gang-related homicides than neighborhoods with 4 to 7 percent unemployment.

segments.title: Debate over whether the gang problem is overstated
segments.summary: Hosts agree there is a gang presence but discuss sociologists who say the gang threat is exaggerated, pointing to a Justice Policy Institute report, and urge listeners to question data sources and who benefits from fear.

segments.title: Why people join gangs
segments.summary: Reasons for joining include peer pressure (gangs recruit in high schools), boredom in communities lacking pools, libraries and youth centers, family problems and a sense of belonging, and gang-run community outreach or job programs.

segments.title: Early gang history: ethnic gangs and Five Points
segments.summary: The hosts recall Gangs of New York and describe 19th-century New York ethnic gangs in Five Points (Irish, Polish, Italian) that fought over turf. They speculate on why ethnic gangs faded and how some former Irish gang members became cops.

segments.title: Car clubs and the founding of the Crips and Bloods
segments.summary: Car clubs of the 1950s and 60s fought with chains and knives. In the 1960s Raymond Washington and a partner founded the Baby Avenues, later the Cribs, in south central Los Angeles, with blue colors taken from Fremont High School. The Bloods formed in the 1970s as a rival coalition, with red colors.

segments.title: Watts Truce and gang nations
segments.summary: Jim Brown helped broker the Watts Truce between the Crips and Bloods, which was largely honored, though infighting among sets continued. The hosts describe Crip and Blood 'nations' as franchise-like networks where local sets compete for territory and drug customers, citing sociologist Mike Carly's research.

segments.title: Drugs, the crack era and Chicago super gangs
segments.summary: Drug dealing transformed gangs in the 1980s and 1990s, especially with crack. Larry Hoover and David Barksdale in Chicago are credited with turning gangs into hierarchical drug businesses, leading to the Black Gangster Disciples. The hosts note the Crip and Blood slang and walks and the Hell's Angels and biker gang comparison.

segments.title: Super gangs, franchising and the People and Folk nations
segments.summary: Super gangs are franchised networks spanning cities; transnational gangs are described as a bigger problem. The hosts list affiliates of the People Nation (Vice Lords, Black P. Stones, Latin Kings, etc.) and the Folk Nation (Gangster Disciples, Maniac Latin Disciples, etc.).

segments.title: Ethnic lines, prison gangs, female and hybrid gangs
segments.summary: Gangs remain divided along ethnic lines because of segregated neighborhoods. Prison gangs are described as criminal college. Female gangs (sister gangs like the Bad Barbies, Harlem Hilton's, Hood Barbies) and co-ed hybrid gangs, which form from mixed factions without fixed colors, are discussed as growing types. Juggalos are listed as a hybrid gang in some states.

segments.title: Gang initiations and recruiting professionals
segments.summary: Initiation methods include killing a cop (described as rare), being jumped in, sexed in, jacked in (committing a theft), running the gauntlet, and games like catching a flag or rag and the sixpence game. Courting in is when sympathetic professionals such as doctors, lawyers or electricians are invited to join. Biker gangs target former military, and gangs have reportedly recruited from the military, with fifty-three gangs represented in the U.S. military.

segments.title: Daily life, gang vs. organized crime, and modern weapons
segments.summary: Gang members' daily life involves drugs and drinking, and higher-tier gangs like MS-13 and M18 do local enforcement for transnational cartels, including smuggling people and mortgage fraud. The hosts say a street gang is a looser, more localized version of organized crime. Modern gangs have access to military-grade weapons, body armor and police gear, sometimes obtained by stealing.

segments.title: Native American and immigrant gangs
segments.summary: Native American gangs emerged in the 1980s and 1990s, driven by identity and protection needs, with Native Americans reportedly experiencing violent crime at double the rate of others and many cases going unpursued by police. Immigrant gangs from Somalia, the Dominican Republic, Sudan, the Caribbean and Jamaica are mentioned, including Somali gangs in Minneapolis and Clarkston, Georgia.

segments.title: Leaving a gang and gang tattoo removal
segments.summary: Myths say leaving a gang requires killing your mother or being beaten out. Former members interviewed in Gangs in America by C. Ronald Huff mostly left by moving, cutting ties or changing their lives. Tattoos are a barrier, and Homeboy Industries offers free gang tattoo removal.

segments.title: Gang prevention, weed and seed, and FBI's dangerous gangs
segments.summary: Economic opportunity is seen as the most effective anti-gang strategy, since police crackdowns just move gangs. The Justice Department's weed and seed program weeds out hardcore members and seeds neighborhoods with jobs, rec centers and libraries. The hosts also discuss the FBI's list of most dangerous gangs, including Florencia 13, Barrio Azteca, Latin Kings, MS-13, and the Trinitarios, and the Mongols biker gang shooting in Waco.

segments.title: Listener mail: five-year-old mother
segments.summary: Listener Brian W. writes about Lena Medina, a Peruvian girl who gave birth at age five, correcting an earlier comment Chuck made in the male puberty episode. The hosts also read the show's contact information.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts thank listeners and give contact details for email, Facebook, Twitter and the website.
